African black oystercatchers nesting along the coastline of southern Africa produce eggs that are incubated at a temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], a thermal regime that sustains embryonic development over a period of approximately 33 days [ab = approximately 33 days]. Field observations indicate that the incubation period can vary between 27 and 39 days depending on local environmental conditions, with the shorter end of the range associated with consistently warm nest microclimates. The newly hatched chicks emerge with a wet weight at birth of about 34 grams [Wwb = about 34 grams], a modest starting mass that is typical of semi-precocial shorebird young. This initial body size, though small, is quickly augmented through intensive biparental provisioning, as both adults engage in foraging and food delivery throughout the early nestling phase. The mass at hatching represents the culmination of yolk-dependent embryonic growth under the extended incubation regime and provides the energetic foundation upon which the rapid post-hatching growth trajectory is built.

Fledging, the developmental milestone at which chicks achieve sustained powered flight, occurs at 38 days after hatching [tx = 38 days after hatching] when ambient conditions are at the species' typical active metabolic temperature of 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C]. This relatively brief post-hatching period to flight capability is characteristic of oystercatchers, reflecting a growth strategy that prioritizes rapid feather development and motor coordination over extended parental dependency. During this phase, nestlings progress from being brooded, downy chicks to fully feathered juveniles capable of escape from terrestrial predators. The timing of fledging is tightly linked to food availability in the intertidal zone, as adults must maintain a high rate of prey delivery to support the energetic demands of feather synthesis and locomotor maturation. Once flight is achieved, the young birds begin to accompany their parents on foraging trips, learning to recognize and handle the mussels, limpets, and other mollusks that constitute their primary diet.

Under the same thermal conditions that define the active metabolic environment of this species, 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C], the time since birth at puberty is approximately 114 days [tp = approximately 114 days]. This interval marks the onset of gonadal maturation and the beginning of physiological readiness for reproduction, though actual breeding is deferred considerably longer. The pubertal transition in Haematopus moquini is accompanied by the development of the adult plumage and the full ossification of the skeletal system, processes that require sustained nutrient intake and the accumulation of body condition. Juveniles that have recently attained sexual maturity often spend their first potential breeding seasons as non-breeding floaters, occupying marginal territories and gradually acquiring the foraging skills necessary to support the energetic costs of egg production and chick rearing. The relatively early achievement of pubertal status compared to the onset of first reproduction suggests that social and ecological constraints, rather than physiological limitations, govern the timing of initial breeding in this long-lived shorebird.

The time since birth at first brood is 1825 days [tR = 1825 days] under the typical thermal conditions of 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C], a five-year delay [tR = a five-year delay] that reflects the protracted period required for territory acquisition, mate pairing, and the development of proficient foraging abilities in this rocky-shore specialist. First-time breeders often select nest sites on the higher portions of the shore, where the risk of tidal overwash is reduced but food availability during low tide may be suboptimal. The interval between puberty and first reproduction, spanning more than four years [tR = more than four years], is among the longest documented for charadriiform birds of comparable body size and suggests that the accumulation of individual experience plays a critical role in reproductive success. Females initiating their first brood typically produce smaller clutches than experienced individuals, and their reproductive output increases with age as they refine their foraging efficiency and nest-site selection. This life-history pattern, characterized by deferred maturity and extended parental care, is consistent with the high adult survival rates and low annual fecundity that typify many large-bodied oystercatcher populations.

Females of this species attain an ultimate wet weight of 670 grams [Wwi = 670 grams], a substantial adult body mass that positions Haematopus moquini as one of the heavier members of the genus. The maximum lifespan recorded for this species, drawing on comparative data from the closely related black oystercatcher Haematopus bachmani, is 35 years [am = 35 years] under the active metabolic temperature regime of 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C], a longevity that underscores the slow pace of life characteristic of this lineage. Clutch size typically consists of 1 to 2 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 1 to 2 eggs per clutch], and pairs produce a single clutch per year [F_R_i = single clutch per year], resulting in a maximum annual reproductive output of up to 2 eggs annually, reflecting a daily reproduction rate of approximately 2 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 2 eggs per year] at 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C]. The combination of high adult survivorship, low fecundity, and extended developmental periods aligns closely with the predictions of slow life-history theory for a relatively large-bodied, territorial shorebird occupying a stable but resource-predictable coastal environment.
